title: The Danger of Reminding Well-Behaved Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2025/02/14/the-danger-of-reminding-well-behaved-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin examines the seemingly harmless habit of giving a favored, capable, or charismatic student a gentle reminder instead of a real consequence when they slip up, and argues it damages both groups of students involved. For the rest of the class, he says the double standard is always noticed even when unspoken, and repeated instances deepen resentment, erode trust in the teacher's fairness, and can even push students toward the misbehavior they're implicitly told is expected of them. For the favored student, he argues the special treatment breeds a dangerous sense of being 'better-than' without the grounding to handle an eventual reckoning with reality, since most will not become the athletes or stars their early treatment implies, leading to a painful fall many never recover from. He frames the teacher's role as uniquely positioned to interrupt both trajectories -- restoring trust and belonging for overlooked students while giving favored ones an early, humbling dose of accountability that protects them later. The piece closes by casting inconsistent leniency, however well-intentioned, as a teacher's participation in the eventual harm of both groups.
points: Even unspoken favoritism toward well-behaved or charismatic students is noticed by classmates and deepens their resentment and mistrust over time.
Repeated leniency toward one student can make others conclude the system is rigged, sometimes prompting them to meet the low expectations they've been implicitly given.
Being treated as special breeds a fragile sense of being 'better-than' in favored students, setting them up for a harder reckoning with reality later in life.
Consistent, equal enforcement of consequences is framed as protective for both the overlooked majority and the favored minority, not punitive.
quotes: One of your smart, capable, polite, well-groomed, athletic, and/or charismatic students accidentally and ever-so-briefly breaks a class rule, and you smile and give them a gentle reminder.

But each time it happens their resentment deepens. Their indifference solidifies. They start to believe that the system is rigged against them. So why bother? Or, better yet, why not give the teacher the misbehavior they expect?
When you’re treated as special because of your looks, athletic ability, intelligence, or any other reason, it’s human nature to start believing that you’re better-than.
This is a dangerous place to be that sets these students up for a terrible fall when they inevitably realize that there are scores of people more talented than them.
You must be mentally strong enough to enforce consequences consistently and equally. You are in a unique position to bring reality and fairness to your little classroom world.
Most assuredly, they will not become a YouTube star. They’re not going to be a professional athlete. They won’t be a tech billionaire. Many will fall off the face of the earth after high school.
